articles.title: Christa Pike speaks out in 1st public statement after failed execution: 'I don't know why I survived'
articles.summary: Christa Pike, who survived a failed execution after two doses of lethal injection drugs, has issued her first public statement describing her painful recover...
articles.body:
Christa Pike is speaking out publicly for the first time since she survived an execution attempt by the state of Tennessee on Sept. 30.

"There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain," Pike said in her first public statement since the execution attempt, which her legal team shared Friday. "My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul."

Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of her classmate, Colleen Slemmer, and spent 30 years on death row. Two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital failed to kill her during the state's execution attempt last month. She was taken to the hospital, where she received lifesaving care.

Slemmer's mother, May Martinez , described the situation as a "mess" and said she was left without justice.

"I'm deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position," Pike said. "I continue to think about my victim's family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured."

Pike's legal team described the outcome as "unprecedented" and said it has raised questions about what happens next in her case.

"I don't know why I survived that night," Pike added. "I don't know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time. And I am holding on to the love and kindness of so many people who have reminded me that I am not alone."

Pike's survival has brought intense scrutiny to Tennessee's execution procedures. Gov. Bill Lee suspended the one remaining execution scheduled for this year, and the state's top prison official, Correction Commissioner Frank Strada, is stepping down at the end of October.

Pike's lawyers said the resignation was "justified, but it does nothing to help Christa now. They said the botched execution "reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person," they said in a statement issued earlier this month, according to ABC News .

Pike has been held at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center since Oct. 10, where she has been behind bars for more than 30 years. She continues to receive medical care in the prison's infirmary.

"I am recovering, and I know that I am getting stronger," her statement read. "But healing is not the same as being okay."

What was Christa Pike's condition after the botched execution?

When Pike arrived at the hospital, her arms were "swollen, burned and blistered," her lawyers wrote in a legal filing on Oct. 2. Her lawyers believe the IV lines were placed incorrectly or her veins burst, so that some or all of the drug went into the tissue of her arms instead of her bloodstream.

Her condition was so severe in the following days, after the execution attempt, that it was believed that she may be brain-dead and could be removed from life support the following day, Randy Spivey, one of her attorneys, said during a press conference on Oct. 7.

"On Tuesday, to the shock of everyone … Christa woke up and began talking," he said.

Spivey added that Pike is feeling "angry and confused" after waking up in the hospital and is still dealing with major physical problems from the failed execution, including a blood clot, pneumonia and swelling that has left her unable to use both of her arms.

"Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery," her legal team wrote in a court filing on Oct. 6.

Dr. Joel Zivot, a medical expert who has consulted with Pike's legal team, told the Associated Press that the latest update "bodes well for a good recovery," but said that the full picture of her long-term health will not be clear for some time.

"She has recovered to a certain degree that she's able to be off a ventilator and able to speak, but in no way would I announce her free of further serious risk," he said. "There's still a lot of bad things that can happen here."

Deborah Denno, a criminologist and professor at Fordham Law School, told the BBC that she was "absolutely astonished" that Pike was conscious and speaking. "They did everything they were supposed to do as part of the execution process, and it simply didn't work," she said. "This has never happened before."

Dr. Zivot told the BBC that her survival was "unusual," adding, "Most people who get lethal injection die from it. In fact, pretty well everyone, except Christa."

Seattle University Law Professor Michael Russo told the Associated Press, "There's nobody else in the history of the death penalty in this country who has gone through what she's been through."

The incident with Pike comes a handful of months after the botched attempt to execute Tony Carruthers . In May, Tennessee stopped the execution of Carruthers after staff placed an IV into his right arm, but were unable to insert a secondary IV line.

All executions in Tennessee are paused for now. Pike's lawyers have called for her sentence to be commuted. State officials have not said whether they will try to execute Pike again, and Gov. Lee has not indicated that he plans to intervene in Pike's case.

Lee had denied Pike's clemency before the execution attempt.

"I think at the very least the governor should commute Ms. Pike's death sentence to a life sentence," attorney Stephen Ferrell told CNN's State of the Union earlier this month. "We don't know what her physical state will be, but it is clear that she has endured a torturous attempt at executing her."

Dr. Zivot said it remains unclear how much pentobarbital entered Pike's system, how much remained in her blood after the injection and what effects she could still experience as she recovers. "I would not, in any way, say at this point that all the big risks are behind her," he said.

Professor Russo doubted whether the Supreme Court would stop the state from trying again on double jeopardy grounds — the constitutional protection against being tried or punished twice for the same offense — should it decide to do so.

He said, "I think what this Supreme Court would say is, her sentence was to die — to be executed — not to suffer an attempt at execution."

"We're in uncharted territory," Robin Maher, executive director of the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center, told USA Today . "The U.S. Supreme Court has not decided whether a second execution attempt would violate the Constitution since 1947. These are questions that have never needed to be asked before, and no one knows the answers."

articles.title: Fears for mature Scots Pines burned by huge Cairngroms wildfire
articles.summary: Experts say some older Scot pine damaged by fire could die removing an important source of seeds
articles.body:
Mature Scots Pine trees may be lost from a Highland landscape hit by a huge summer wildfire, experts fear.

Forestry and Land Scotland say the blaze around Glenmore in the Cairngorms may have led to the loss of many so-called "granny pines" which have matured over centuries.

They say their loss removes important seed sources and makes it more difficult for the species to regenerate.

However, the Scottish government agency said there were many encouraging signs of natural recovery among other species following the fire.

It burned through about 10 sq miles of forest and moorland near Aviemore in July and August.

More stories from the Highlands and Islands

News from the Highlands and Islands on BBC Sounds

Forestry and Land Scotland staff who have been monitoring the site have recorded birch, rowan and willow regenerating from surviving stems and root systems.

Large areas of hillside have also been observed turning green again as grasses, bracken and blaeberry begin to make a comeback.

The agency said this was particularly apparent where moisture had remained in the soil or where fire intensity was lower.

Deer and capercaillie are now being regularly spotted in the fire damaged area, attracted by the new grass growth.

FLS forestry management and stewardship forester Eelco de Jong said the recovery of broadleaf vegetation was promising with lots of birch, rowan and willow expected to grow back quickly.

However, he warned that there were "significant challenges" ahead because of organic soil layers being badly affected and due to damage to the area's renowned Scots pine.

He said: "The concern is many of the oldest 'granny pines' could be lost, removing important seed sources and habitat for species such as capercaillie."

"Some of these veteran trees were more than 100 or 200 years old and, where losses occur, it could take centuries for trees of a similar stature to return to the landscape."

articles.title: How a passenger's confession helped convict her cousin of murder
articles.summary: Simon Richardson hit cyclist Michael Mullins with his car and dragged him along for over a mile.
articles.body:
Warning: This article contains distressing content

One afternoon in April, a children's nursery worker approached her manager in what she described as an hysterical state.

Gabrielle Debotte said she had something serious to tell Nicola Goddard, adding: "You're going to hate me and I'm going to lose my job."

What the 27-year-old said next proved a turning point in the investigation into the death of popular head teacher Michael Mullins, who had been struck by a car the previous day and dragged under its wheels for more than a mile.

Debotte told the astonished Goddard she not only knew who was responsible for hitting the 56-year-old as he cycled home from work, but she witnessed what happened from the passenger seat.

That night, having initially been treated as a suspect, she sat in the interview suite at Stretford Police Station and named her cousin, 35-year-old former mechanic Simon Richardson, as the driver.

Thanks in part to the evidence provided by Debotte, Richardson was found guilty of murder after a two-week trial at Manchester's Minshull Street Crown Court.

The contrasts between the lives of the killer and his victim were stark.

Less than a month before he struck the head teacher, Richardson was freed from prison.

He had served 47 days on remand awaiting sentence for stalking, harassment, threats to damage property and assaulting an emergency worker, and was freed on 26 March after being sentenced to a non-custodial community order.

In the following weeks, he was "sofa-surfing" between various addresses - including the home Debotte shared with her father in Altrincham, Greater Manchester.

In contrast, the head teacher had spent the past 17 years leading Stretford Grammar School, where he was known as a man of "unshakeable principles and a compassionate leader".

To his family, he was a beloved husband, father and grandfather, who "truly excelled" in his "role as grandad".

He was a lover of sport and remained physically fit, regularly cycling the 19 miles between the school and his home in Northwich, Cheshire.

At 17:35 BST on 20 April, he changed into his cycling clothes, put on his helmet and set off as normal.

Detectives would later be able to plot his journey via his Apple watch, which monitored his speed, location and heart rate.

Not far from the cyclist's starting point, a black Volvo XC90 was already catching the attention of other drivers as it sped "erratically" along the semi-rural roads on the outskirts of Trafford and north-east Cheshire.

It was being driven by Richardson, who had agreed to give his cousin a lift from Altrincham to a beauty salon in Lymm to pick up some weight-loss jabs.

In court, Debotte told jurors Richardson had been driving very fast and when she told him to slow down, his only response was to "smirk" and claim he was "a professional driver".

At 18:07, the car reached a junction in Warburton, Trafford, which connected Dunham Road with Paddock Lane.

According to Debotte and other witnesses, the Volvo ignored stop signs and road markings on Dunham Road as it attempted to turn left.

Debotte told the court she shouted "bike" three times, but Richardson made no attempt to slow down or brake before the Volvo smashed into the left side of the cyclist.

Witnesses saw the head teacher being thrown into the air while his bike, phone, part of his helmet and a wireless earphone were scattered across the road.

Witness Leon Dalziel-Bush, who saw the crash from his own vehicle, said the Volvo was going at such speed that "by the time I processed what had happened, it had gone".

Dalziel-Bush and others got out to help, but after searching in ditches and grass verges, they realised the cyclist was nowhere to be seen.

Richardson, who according to Debotte, stopped for a "split-second" before accelerating away, was already guilty of very serious criminal offences.

What happened over the next four minutes or so, prosecutors argued in court, made him a murderer.

The prosecution case hinged on whether it could prove Richardson was aware the cyclist was trapped and suffering increasingly appalling injuries just inches from his feet.

Phil Barnes KC, prosecuting, told the jury that many of them would know what it feels like to drive "with a flat tyre, or with wheels that are slightly out of balance or misaligned".

"Now imagine driving your car, at north of 60mph, with a fully grown human being wedged in the suspension and steering assembly of one of your wheels," he said.

Barnes had suggested it "must have been obvious" to Richardson that the 56-year-old was there, but "he carried on regardless", knowing his actions "were in all likelihood killing the man beneath his feet".

But, thanks to Debotte's workplace revelation, the case was built on much more than that simple premise.

When she gave her statement to police, she described a scene of absolute shock and panic in the car, complete with "screaming and crying".

"I had never seen anything like that in my life," she said, adding: "I still have visions of it."

She also recalled how "moaning" could clearly be heard from beneath the Volvo as it sped away and that Richardson blurted out: "He's under the car."

Detectives would be able to prove, via watch and phone data, that his car had stopped on Wet Gate Lane in Lymm a short time after the collision.

The data showed the car had remained stationary on the rural country lane for about 90 seconds, as the cyclist was still clinging to life.

Debotte's account of those moments was absolutely crucial to proving Richardson was guilty of more than causing death by dangerous driving and failing to stop.

She said as she sat "frozen" in the passenger seat, he got out, walked around the front of the vehicle and tried to pull the head teacher free.

When the first attempt failed, he returned to the driver's seat and moved the steering wheel to try and free the wheels.

Debotte said Richardson got out again and crouched down to make another attempt to pull his victim free.

After failing again, he started the engine and drove further along Wet Gate Lane.

CCTV from a nearby farm showed the car swerving from side-to-side before the cyclist was finally thrown clear on to a grass verge.

From the position he was found, prosecutors were also able to say that the car must have driven over his body when it reversed and turned back towards the main road, all but ensuring his injuries were fatal.

The court was shown distressing evidence in support of Debotte's account, including images of a sharp-angled tyre mark left in a pool of blood where the car had stopped.

The jury heard the mark could only have been made by the wheels being turned while the car was stationary.

Nobody was around when the 56-year-old was thrown from the vehicle and left to his fate, but a few minutes later, motorcylist Andrew Beasant-Roberts found him after following a trail of blood from close to the crash site just over a mile away.

Beasant-Roberts made a 999 call and tried to perform CPR, but it was too late.

Detectives later found CCTV footage which showed Richardson and Debotte at Lymm Service Station minutes later, filling the car with petrol.

The pair then finished the errand they initially set out to do and picked up Debotte's jabs from the salon in Lymm.

She was dropped off at her Altrincham home at 18:45, where she stayed until she left for work again the following morning.

After dropping her off, Richardson quickly arranged to swap the Volvo for a silver Ford Transit work van with an associate.

He returned to Debotte's house in the van with a friend and the pair came and went from the house throughout the night.

Debotte said the men had been "laughing and joking" while listening to music and drinking her father's alcohol, but Richardson also lost his temper when she asked them to leave, punching a hole in plasterwork and kicking a chair.

She said there were no direct threats, but Richards outlined an account for her to give to police if they came knocking, which she wrote down in a note-taking app on her phone.

It included instructions to say she had lent Richardson her bank card on the day before and had not seen him again until late on the day of the crash.

However, Debotte said she already "knew she was going to talk to the police" and would be telling the truth.

In court, Debotte accepted she "absolutely" could have done more to alert the police to what had happened earlier, but her decision to seek them out before anyone else knew she had been in the vehicle allowed them to treat her as a witness.

Based on her description of the van, Greater Manchester Police officers found it the following day in Failsworth.

Despite knowing he was being tailed by a trained pursuit driver, Richardson tried to flee, first speeding through narrow residential streets and then making a final futile attempt to escape on foot.

He has never given a public account of his actions on 20 April.

The court heard he declined to answer police questions and on 22 October, at the conclusion of the prosecution case, the jury were told he would not be giving evidence in his own defence.

Jaime Hamilton KC, defending, explained while questioning witnesses that Richardson denied he knew the cyclist was under the car and denied he had got out of the vehicle on Wet Gate Lane.

However, the evidence and the testimony of Debotte meant the jury were sure he was guilty of more than a serious driving offence and fully convinced he had made the conscious decision to drag a helpless and well-respected family man to a most horrific death.

Richardson is due to be sentenced on Monday.

articles.title: Wildlife body loses lynx reintroduction High Court challenge
articles.summary: Lynx UK Trust wants to release the felines into Kielder Forest.
articles.body:
An organisation trying to bring lynx back to northern England has lost a High Court challenge.

Lynx UK Trust applied for a three-year trial in 2022 which could have seen three of the animals from Sweden released into Kielder Forest, but it was refused by Natural England.

The trust challenged the environmental body over the refusal to proceed to a full assessment but Ms Justice Obi dismissed the claim, saying: "On Natural England's understanding of the law, the proposed release could not lawfully be implemented."

In July, Northumberland County Council backed a motion stating it would not support any effort to release lynx into the wild.

The big cats have been extinct in the wild in the UK for centuries, but plans have been made to reintroduce the animals in the hope of helping biodiversity and controlling deer populations.

A year-long social consultation by the Missing Lynx Project found 72% of people in the North East supported the reintroduction of the big cats , but opponents believe lynx could attack sheep and other livestock.

Non-aligned Rothbury councillor Steven Bridgett, who proposed the council's motion, called the High Court result excellent.

Lynx UK Trust originally applied in 2017 for six lynx to be released into the forest as part of a five-year trial, but this was refused by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) the following year.

The group then submitted a revised proposal in 2022 for a three-year trial involving the release of the three lynx from Sweden.

But that was also refused by Natural England the same year, with the body claiming such a release was prohibited by the Dangerous Wild Animals Act 1976 (DWAA), which makes it an offence to release certain animals into the wild.

Lynx UK Trust challenged the refusal in the High Court, with its lawyers claiming the animals could still be released under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 (WCA).

The WCA allows authorities to issue licences for the release of animals which are not "ordinarily resident" in the wild in the UK, despite the terms of DWAA.

The trust also argued at the hearing earlier this month the terms of the DWAA had been "impliedly repealed" by the terms of the WCA.

Natural England and Defra opposed the claim.

In a 16-page judgment, Obi said: "Properly construed, the DWAA continues to apply to lynx as a scheduled dangerous wild animal.

"I am unable to accept either the claimant's primary submission that the Act ceases to apply upon deliberate release pursuant to a licence under... the WCA, or its alternative submission that the relevant provisions have been impliedly repealed by the later enactment of the WCA."

articles.title: A Pennsylvania family has owned Penn's Cave since 1908 and expanded its land to protect its water; 118 years later, the 1,400-acre attraction with a cavern, wildlife park and airport is seeking a new owner
articles.summary: After 118 years under the ownership of one family, America's only all-water cave and wildlife park has been put up for sale.
articles.body: After 118 years under the ownership of one family, America's only all-water cave and wildlife park has been put up for sale. The move begins the search for a new owner to take over the historic 1,400-acre property in central Pennsylvania. The Campbell family, which first bought Penn's Cave in 1908, announced the sale through press release services and property firm Lusk and Associates Sotheby's International Realty. The property is located in Centre Hall and has an asking price of $34 million (£26 million). The large estate includes the limestone cave system, a farm and wildlife park, a private airport, and large areas of surrounding land built up over four generations. Offers for the property began in October. This is the first time in more than a century that the well-known tourist attraction has been put up for sale.Four generations of environmental stewardshipThe natural attraction first opened to visitors nearly 150 years ago, but its modern history began when the Campbell family bought it in 1908. Over the next 118 years, four generations of the family worked to expand the property. They bought nearby land mainly to protect the local water supply and preserve the underground water system. The cave depends on an underground river that releases up to 11 million gallons of clean water every day. The family's environmental protection efforts were aimed at keeping the water clean and protecting the delicate limestone cave formations and the surrounding natural environment. According to statements released by Lusk and Associates Sotheby's International Realty, the family made environmental protection a priority while slowly growing the business. Over the years, the property developed from a small local cave tour business into a 1,400-acre estate. It now includes wildlife protection areas, farmland, tourist attractions, and transport facilities.A uniquely aquatic cave experienceThe main attraction remains the limestone cave, which is recognised as the only cave in North America where visitors take the entire tour by boat. Visitors travel along an underground river that passes through large natural chambers filled with stalactites, stalagmites, and flowing rock formations. Beyond the cave, the estate also includes a large farm and wildlife park. It is home to native North American animals such as bison, elk, wolves, and bears, as well as exotic species. Guided bus tours take visitors across the property, where they can see animals living in large open spaces designed to look like their natural homes. The property also has a working private airstrip measuring 2,600 feet, known as Penn's Cave Airport. It provides direct air access to the site. Other visitor attractions include a visitor centre, gift shop, gem-panning stations, a large plant maze, and off-road mountain jeep trails across the 1,400-acre property.State park evaluation and property futureNews of the sale attracted immediate attention across Pennsylvania. State officials have also started discussing whether the property could become part of the public conservation system. According to reports published by the Centre Daily Times, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro confirmed that state officials are looking into whether buying Penn's Cave and Wildlife Park would be a suitable addition to the state park system. State Representative Kerry Benninghoff had earlier supported state involvement. He described the possible loss of public access as a major concern for the local community and its heritage. Despite the planned sale, the Campbell family confirmed that public tours, animal care, and visitor programmes will continue as usual. The family said keeping the business running without disruption is its main priority during the change in ownership. "Continuing the experience we're known for is our greatest priority throughout this transition," the Campbell family stated in a joint press release. The family also explained that the decision to sell is focused on "preserving the business and finding the next steward of the land who can see the immense potential of the property and continue the legacy."You use AI every day. articles.summary: DHS confirmed the wrong-way driver who killed University of New Haven hockey captain Ryan O'Shea had illegally reentered the United States twice.
articles.body: A 21-year-old college hockey captain who dreamed of becoming a police officer was killed in a wrong-way crash involving a Mexican national who repeatedly entered the United States illegally after previously being removed, the Department of Homeland Security confirmed to Fox News Digital. Ryan O'Shea, a senior at the University of New Haven, was driving south on Interstate 91 in North Haven late Oct. 16 when a Chevrolet Silverado traveling the wrong way slammed head-on into his Honda Accord, Connecticut State Police said. According to the State Police accident summary, 31-year-old Guillermo Carmona-Lopez of Bridgeport was driving the Silverado. ICE LODGES DETAINER FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED IN WRONG-WAY MARYLAND CRASH THAT KILLED MOM, DAUGHTER The crash sent O'Shea's car into another lane, where it was struck by a Jeep before moving onto the right shoulder and being hit by a third vehicle. O'Shea suffered fatal injuries and was pronounced dead at the scene. Carmona-Lopez was taken to Yale New Haven Hospital with serious, life-threatening injuries, while three other people suffered minor injuries. ILLEGAL ALIEN ORDERED REMOVED YEARS AGO CHARGED IN CRASH THAT KILLED NEWLY ENGAGED 23-YEAR-OLD TEACHER DHS told Fox News Digital that Carmona-Lopez entered the U.S. illegally multiple times despite previously being removed and receiving a final order of removal. "In May 2013, Border Patrol arrested Guillermo Carmona-Lopez, a criminal illegal alien from Mexico, after he illegally entered the country," a DHS spokesperson said. "Carmona-Lopez was issued an expedited removal and was removed from the country." articles.title: What the Ruthless Fellas are watching ahead of the midterms
articles.summary: The “Ruthless Podcast" hosts share which races and early results they’ll be watching on election night as the critical 2026 midterms approach.
articles.body: The "Ruthless Podcast" Fellas have some of the best political insights in the game, and we asked them what they'll be looking at ahead of Tuesday's critical midterms. Control of the House and U.S. Senate are at stake as Democrats try to take back Congress after Republicans swept the White House and both chambers in 2024. From what polls are or aren't reliable, to the races sparking the most interest, to what the media continues to get wrong in political coverage, the Fellas have your answers. MEET THE RUTHLESS PODCAST FELLAS Comfortably Smug If you could only watch one race on election night, which is it, and what’s the first thing you check when the polls close? Maine Senate. Susan Collins has an incredible ability to lose every poll and win every election, thus far. Will she be able to overcome the atmosphere of this election is a huge question. The first thing I check when polls close is early exits, which I find to be the most reliable and illuminating data on election night. What’s the one number you trust more than the polls (early vote, turnout, special election overperformance, fundraising, something else), and what threshold would make you feel good or bad about your side? EARLY EXIT numbers are the most trustworthy! Dems always talk about a red mirage followed by a blue wave on election nights. If early exits don't go Republicans' way, it will be a bad night. What is the media overhyping going into the midterms, and what is it ignoring? The media is overhyping Barack Obama as a candidate surrogate. He stumped for Hillary [Clinton], he stumped for Kamala [Harris], and they both lost. Obama has no coattails. Which poll, pundit, or conventional wisdom do you not believe, and why? I do not trust any polls. Early exits are the only reliable source of data. John Ashbrook TRUMP AND TOP DEMOCRATS TARGET KEY STATES AHEAD OF ELECTION DAY If you could only watch one race on election night, which is it, and what’s the first thing you check when the polls close? Ohio Senate. Watch returns in the 50 counties where President Trump outperformed Mitt Romney by 10 or more points. What’s the one number you trust more than the polls (early vote, turnout, special election overperformance, fundraising, something else), and what threshold would make you feel good or bad about your side? [Mike] Rogers' performance in Oakland County is a number to watch. And also his share of the vote in Michigan’s Seventh Congressional District. He could come out on top if he outperforms his 2024 vote totals in those areas. FOX NEWS UNVEILS 2026 MIDTERM ELECTION COVERAGE PLANS What is the media overhyping going into the midterms, and what is it ignoring? The media always overhypes late-breaking vibes and underreports multi-year, local level grassroots operations. Good candidates can overperform the environment with competent campaigns. Which poll, pundit, or conventional wisdom do you not believe, and why? Public polling is often less reliable than professional private surveys based on years of state and local level expertise. So I’m always skeptical of public polling. But the one thing they’ve captured accurately is the difficult environment Republican candidates are currently navigating. Michael Duncan WATCH: ‘RUTHLESS’ SHARES AN INSIDER’S GUIDE TO ELECTION NIGHT If you could only watch one race on election night, which is it, and what’s the first thing you check when the polls close? articles.title: Syria dreamed of a new dawn after Assad, but economic misery clouds its future
articles.summary: Nearly two years after Bashar al-Assad was ousted, Syrians who had hoped for a better life under President Ahmed al-Sharaa are still struggling to afford
articles.body: Nearly two years after Bashar al-Assad was ousted, Syrians who had hoped for a better life under President Ahmed al-Sharaa are still struggling to afford basic necessities. Rising food, fuel and electricity costs are deepening an economic crisis that has fuelled public anger against the new administration.The government's inability to ease the financial burden on households was laid bare in September, when a sharp increase in fuel prices triggered widespread protests. The unrest forced authorities to partially roll back the decision, according to a Reuters report.The government had raised diesel prices by 40 per cent on September 14, taking them to 175 Syrian pounds per litre from 125 pounds. It also increased the prices of 95-octane petrol by 28 per cent to 195 pounds, 90-octane petrol by 26 per cent to 185 pounds, and household and industrial gas by around 9 per cent.The increases triggered demonstrations across Syria is the most widespread since Assad's fall. Protesters burned tyres, blocked key roads, including the highway linking Damascus to Aleppo, and disrupted crude tanker convoys heading towards refineries in central Syria. Some demanded the dismissal of the energy and economy ministers and the head of the Syrian Petroleum Company."We don't want higher wages. All we want is lower diesel and other fuel prices," news agency Reuters reported citing protestor Yasser Salim in Aleppo.Another protester, Bassam al-Ali, appealed directly to al-Sharaa. "Border crossings bring in millions of dollars. We don't want new roundabouts or malls. We just want to live," he said.Days later, in mid September, Syria's energy minister Mohammed al-Bashir announced a partial retreat, offering diesel at three different prices depending on its intended use. Locally produced diesel would be sold at 115 Syrian pounds per litre for heating, agriculture and other eligible users. A second grade, sourced with the help of what Bashir described as "friendly countries", would cost 150 pounds for productive and service sectors and heavy machinery. The standard grade would remain at 175 pounds per litre, while petrol and gas prices would remain unchanged.Bashir said the government was selling standard diesel below its production cost of 206 pounds per litre. He also announced plans to restart small local refineries, known in Syria as "burners", with a combined crude-processing capacity of up to 35,000 barrels per day. The move followed a meeting with al-Sharaa over the fuel crisis.The protests were the latest indication of the economic pressures confronting the new administration. In a separate report by BBC , several Syrians struggling to afford food, pay electricity bills and find employment said their financial circumstances had deteriorated since Assad's removal.The United Nations Development Programme estimates that 90 per cent of Syrians live below the poverty line, compared with around a third before the civil war began in 2011.The government has cut long-standing subsidies as part of an austerity drive. The price of bread, a staple food, has increased tenfold, while electricity prices have risen by several hundred per cent for some consumers. Higher fuel costs have also pushed up transportation expenses and added pressure on farmers, according to the BBC.The administration has adjusted public sector salaries and pensions, but rising prices have eroded the benefit of the additional payments.For many households, even basic food has become difficult to afford. Fatima Saleh Eid, a 50-year-old cleaner in a suburb of Damascus, told the BBC that her family had reduced its food consumption and could no longer afford meat."We eat more sparingly now. We can't afford chicken anymore, nor meat. We only eat vegetables but even [that is] expensive," she said.Another resident, Nabil al-Remhein, a 63-year-old pensioner said that his family had been reduced to one meal a day. None of his four adult children could find work. His electricity bill accounted for around a third of the family's income, forcing them to cut back on lighting and switch off their refrigerator for about five hours a day."We're now having only one meal a day. It's tragic," he said.Marwan Bashour, a 68-year-old pensioner, said his monthly income was around $90, equivalent to the public sector minimum wage. He said he had been forced to borrow money and sell household belongings to meet expenses, as per BBC."Sometimes I borrow money, sometimes I sell things from my house, like an old pot or plates that we never used, gifts that were given to us. I've even had to sell furniture," he said.The difficulties have also extended to access to healthcare. One man in his 20s told that his family could no longer afford medicines for his father, who had a heart condition. A young woman said she and her four children could afford a proper meal only once every two days.Syria's economic difficulties have been compounded by disruptions to fuel supplies. Its energy ministry spokesperson Abdulhamid Salat said the September price increases were a temporary measure driven by higher global procurement costs and the country's heavy dependence on imports. He said prices could be revised up or down depending on changing conditions, news agency Reuters reported.Syria imported around 60,000 barrels per day of Russian crude this year, although Damascus told Washington it was willing to sharply reduce those purchases. Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have reduced production, prompting Moscow to restrict petrol and diesel exports.The three-month closure of Syria's largest refinery, Baniyas, for comprehensive maintenance has further increased dependence on expensive imports. Bashir said the overhaul was expected to raise its refining capacity to around 130,000 barrels per day.Since February, Syrian diesel prices have more than doubled, while 95-octane petrol prices have risen around 86 per cent. Over roughly the same period, benchmark Brent crude gained around 44 per cent.The economic crisis comes as the country continues to deal with the destruction left by more than 13 years of civil war. The conflict killed around half a million people and displaced half the population. Large parts of Syria remain in ruins, while many families unable to afford rent live in partially destroyed buildings.The World Bank estimates Syria's reconstruction costs at $216 billion, making the task of rebuilding heavily dependent on foreign assistance and investment.The new administration has secured some international gains. Sanctions imposed during the Assad era have been lifted, and the United States has removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism. However, the economic benefits of these developments have yet to translate into relief for many households.Dr Haid Haid, a Syrian columnist and consulting fellow at Chatham House, said that a "significant portion of the population" was worse off than before Assad's fall. He described the economic crisis as "one of the most dangerous issues" facing the government."Part of [the crisis] is related to the lack of [financial] resources and the legacy left by the former regime," he said."But it's also the direct impact of the new policies that are moving [Syria] towards a liberal and free-market sort of economy, which don't take into account the impact on people".Syrian economist Samir Aita, who heads the Paris-based Circle of Arab Economists, said the government's handling of public expectations and economic policies had contributed to the crisis."It's unsustainable. If they don't change, I fear chaos," he said.However, some Syrians remain willing to give the new administration time. BBC quoted Abu Mahmoud, a cab driver, who said,"They inherited the country bankrupt, so people need to be patient. Things don't happen overnight."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: US Midterms 2026: Trump reschedules Iowa, Kansas campaign rallies for Sunday after cancellations
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump alters campaign plans to hold in-person rallies in Iowa and Kansas this Sunday, amid competitive Senate races and recent cancellations. Learn about his strategic moves and upcoming events as the midterm elections approach.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump will hold campaign rallies in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday, reversing an earlier decision to cancel the events as Republicans seek to retain their Senate majority in the November midterm elections, people familiar with his plans told AP.The Iowa rally will take place in Cedar Rapids instead of Dubuque, while the Kansas event has also been moved to Sunday.Trump had initially planned to visit Salina, Kansas, on Saturday and Dubuque, Iowa, on Sunday. The Republican National Committee later announced that the in-person events would be replaced by telephone rallies as part of a 72-hour campaign push to reach voters nationwide.The latest arrangements will allow Trump to hold both in-person rallies alongside the phone events.Trump rejected suggestions that the Kansas cancellation was linked to his health or fatigue. Speaking to reporters on Thursday, he said he did not need to visit the state because Republican Senator Roger Marshall was performing well.“I feel perfect,” Trump said, adding that he did not feel he had to go to Kansas.Telephone rallies are generally shorter and cheaper to organise than in-person events. Trump typically speaks for about 10 minutes during these calls, compared with the longer speeches he delivers at campaign rallies.Both Iowa and Kansas have competitive Senate races that could help determine control of the chamber. Trump has already visited the states this month to campaign for Marshall and Republican Iowa Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, who currently serves in the House of Representatives.Vice President JD Vance also campaigned for Marshall in Kansas earlier this week. He had been scheduled to visit St Cloud, Minnesota, on Friday for a news conference on the administration's anti-fraud efforts, but the appearance was cancelled following a scheduling change.In a Friday radio interview, Trump praised Marshall for supporting policies benefiting Kansas farmers, including the expansion of tax-free use of red-dyed diesel. articles.title: Canada stops using 'avalanche dogs' for rescues in Rocky Mountains, stirring outrage
articles.summary: A 55-year-old dog rescue programme that has found missing hikers and children in the Canadian wilderness was axed as part of government budget cuts.
articles.body:
Scott Ward can still recall the relief he saw on parents' faces when a search and rescue dog he was working with found their children safe in Canada's vast and heavily wooded Banff National Park.

Another time, his canine partner led him hiking up a steep mountainside for two hours until they reached a man with a broken leg who was close to dying from hypothermia.

Now 73 and retired, Ward spent 17 years as a dog handler in the wilderness of the Canadian Rocky Mountains, work he described as gratifying.

Over the years, the rescue programme was cut back to just one person in the role, and Ward was shocked when he heard recently that Parks Canada will end the programme entirely as of this month.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's government is making broad funding cuts to Canada's public service, and Parks Canada announced last week that hundreds of their employees will soon be laid off.

The agency confirmed the news to the BBC, calling it a "difficult decision" to axe its sole dog handler position out of Banff National Park, one of the most rugged parts of Canada that welcomes more than four million visitors each year from around the world.

It added it is part of its efforts to modernise its law enforcement branch, and that "search and rescue operations will continue to be delivered" through other means.

Cutting this one role has stirred public outrage, with more than 5,000 people signing a petition since Tuesday to restore it.

William Stevenson, the Conservative Member of Parliament for the Banff area who started the petition, says he welcomes tighter government spending, but that this cut could harm public safety.

"How could they possibly make such a bad choice in where to cut?" he told the BBC.

The BBC has asked Parks Canada about how much the canine search and rescue programme cost to administer.

For 55 years, the government used rescue dogs in the Canadian Rocky Mountains who were trained to trace "everything", Ward said, from a small paper clip to shell casings to a human body.

After avalanches, a common winter hazard in the area, they were called upon to search for trapped hikers or skiers underneath heavy mounds of snow.

"It saves probers hours and hours of standing shoulder to shoulder and poking in the snow, and also exposing themselves to secondary avalanche hazards," Ward said.

In the summer, they helped find children who got lost, often after wandering away from their parents' campsites.

"We lost a huge public safety and staff safety resource," he said.

Other countries still rely on canines, often called "avalanche dogs", for mountain search and rescue, including Italy .

The last dog in Parks Canada's programme, a German Shephard named Leroy, was retired in August.

For the seven years that he was on the job, Leroy helped track 156 people, find 57 who were lost in the wilderness, and solve two murders in Banff.

A new canine was trained and ready for duty before Parks Canada gave notice last week that the programme would be eliminated as part of recent C$145m ($104m; £78m) budget cuts to Parks Canada, local newspaper Rocky Mountain Outlook reported.

Along with his petition, Stevenson also raised the issue in Canada's parliament during a late sitting on Thursday.

In response, Ryan Turnball, a Liberal MP and the parliamentary secretary for finance, said the government is focused on reducing Canada's deficit and "ensuring public funds support growth, resilience and the well-being of Canadians".

Stevenson said he will continue to push on the issue, and has asked for a sit-down meeting with Parks Canada's CEO.

As for Ward, he hopes that the programme will soon be restored.

He recalled a quote that was often uttered by an old park warden who trained him: "You can make an armpit smell like a lilac bush and you can put a man on the moon, but nothing can replace the nose of the avalanche dog."

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Shiv Sena MLA Sanjay Gaikwad on Friday expressed regret over his remarks, days after asking people not to attend the funerals of farmers who die by suicide. He had urged crop growers to support their families and not abandon them.Gaikwad claimed that he had not, in fact, mentioned farmers in his remarks and that he himself came from a farmer's family."My statement was about those who take drugs, ruin their households, and commit suicide....It was misinterpreted and created a controversy. Still, if farmers across Maharashtra and my senior leaders have been hurt, I humbly express my regret," he said.This comes as Maharashtra deputy chief minister Eknath Shinde is reportedly upset over Gaikwad's remarks and has proposed his suspension from the party.When asked about Shinde's decision, Gaikwad said, "No comments."Earlier on Tuesday, Gaikwad had said that people should not attend the funerals of farmers who die by suicide.If nobody attended these funerals and animals fed on the deceased person's body, it might make others contemplating suicide realise the consequences and stop them from taking the extreme step, the MLA of the Eknath Shinde-led party had said.“If you (farmers) have a problem, write to the government, your MLA or your MP. Otherwise, let me know about your difficulties, and everyone will help you. But by taking your own life and leaving your children helpless, you are, in a way, punishing them,” he said.“You take the seven sacred rounds with your wife, vow to stand by her for seven lifetimes and promise to look after your children. Yet, if you end your life halfway through, what happens to those promises?” he asked.The Shiv Sena legislator said he had always maintained in his speeches that if someone died by suicide, no one should attend that person's funeral.“Only when people realise that their bodies may be eaten by animals and understand what happens to their remains will they stop committing suicide,” Gaikwad said.This is not the first time when Gaikwad has been surrounded with controversies. articles.title: G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister
articles.summary: European foreign ministers refused to be pictured with Sergei Lavrov at the summit being held in Atlanta.
articles.body:
European diplomats have refused to stand for an official photo with Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in the US, leading to the American hosts cancelling the planned picture.

Two officials confirmed to the BBC the cancellation of the so-called family photo scheduled for Friday morning, which would usually include representatives from all the nations in attendance.

The meeting, which gathers top diplomats from the world's biggest economies, is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Ukraine is not not a G20 member but has been invited to similar meetings in recent years. However, Ukraine was not invited to this meeting.

Relations between Ukraine and the US have been particularly tense this month, with a diplomatic standoff between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and US President Donald Trump over Kyiv's strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is present and a diplomatic source confirmed the UK was among the countries which refused to participate in the picture.

One British official said: "The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and we are not about to change that".

A US official said the photo was cancelled "after it became clear some of the delegations were unwilling to participate in a joint photo".

"Rather than allow a ceremonial photo opportunity to become a diplomatic distraction, the US decided to forgo the photo and keep the focus on the substantive discussions," the official said.

In contrast to Ukraine, relations between the US and Russia appear to have partially thawed in recent weeks, as Trump waived some sanctions and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the American market.

The move comes as Trump attempts to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of mid-term elections at the start of November, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.

Ukraine and its European allies have heavily criticised Trump's deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Zelensky called it "a gift" to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".

Trump said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table in the war between Russia and Ukraine.

Putin has said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, is willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and currently controls approximately a fifth of Ukrainian territory.

Moscow has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.

articles.title: Indian-origin Shruti Chopra becomes first South Asian woman to ring LSE bell in 40 years
articles.summary: Indian-origin Shruti Tripathi Chopra, editor-in-chief of Dow Jones publications Financial News and Private Equity News, made history at the London Stock
articles.body: Indian-origin Shruti Tripathi Chopra, editor-in-chief of Dow Jones publications Financial News and Private Equity News, made history at the London Stock Exchange. She became the first South Asian woman to ring its closing bell since the ceremony returned after a 40-year absence.The ceremony was held in London on Thursday, to celebrate the second annual South Asian Power Brokers list, which recognises influential South Asian leaders in global finance and business.The event brought together prominent figures from the City, including London Stock Exchange chief executive Dame Julia Hoggett, Brookfield's Private Equity Group vice-chair Sir Ron Kalifa, Paul, Weiss vice-chair Neel Sachdev and UK Office for Investment chief executive Parminder Kohli.British Fashion Council chair Pavita Cooper, Deutsche Bank's UK and Ireland chief executive Vathany Vijayaratna and Cobra Beer founder Lord Karan Bilimoria were also present.The gathering recognised the contribution of South Asian leaders to financial services, investment, law and business. It also highlighted the importance of representation, mentorship and creating opportunities for future generations.The occasion was particularly meaningful for Chopra as it coincided with Karva Chauth, a traditional Hindu festival observed by many married women. She was joined by her in-laws, who are visiting London. Her mother-in-law was also observing the fast.Speaking about the significance of the occasion, Chopra said, “The South Asian leaders standing alongside me on the balcony of the London Stock Exchange collectively oversee billions of dollars. Yet when I asked how many had imagined, at the start of their careers, that they would one day stand on that balcony being celebrated for their professional success and South Asian heritage, not a single hand went up."She further added, “Ringing the closing bell at the London Stock Exchange matters because it sends a powerful message about who belongs at the very top of global finance. We are not just celebrating extraordinary achievement. We are changing what the next generation believes is possible. It was an immense honour to stand alongside some of the most influential figures in the industry and demonstrate that our South Asian heritage is not something we have to leave at the door to succeed. It is part of our success.”The ceremony was followed by a Diwali reception celebrating the South Asian business community and its contribution to the UK economy.Chopra was awarded the Freedom of the City of London in December 2025 in recognition of her contribution to financial journalism and efforts to promote diversity in the City. She is the first woman and the first person of colour to lead Financial News and Private Equity News in their nearly 30-year history.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.body: I'm a side sleeper, no matter how hard I try to sleep on my back. Side sleeping isn't necessarily bad, but it's made it a challenge to find a pillow that cradles my head and neck without leaving me stiff or achy in the morning — until now. After sleeping on the Layla BioCrystal Side Sleeper Pillow, I finally found what I would consider to be the ideal setup for side sleepers. Now through Nov. 26, FOX readers can get an extra 20% off the sale price of both BioCrystal pillows with code FOXDEAL. That brings the Side Sleeper Pillow down to $119 and the Classic Pillow to $111. Layla BioCrystal Side Sleeper Pillow: $119 (37% off) with code FOXDEAL Original price: $189 Side sleepers know how difficult it can be to find a comfortable position and stay there. Layla's BioCrystal Side Sleeper Pillow strikes a comfortable balance between softness and support. Its adjustable loft lets you choose among 7, 6 or 5 inches, while the U-shaped cutout gives your shoulder more room to rest naturally. Layla recommends washing it in warm water on a gentle cycle with like colors and tumble drying it on low. Do not use bleach. The four foam layers should only be spot-cleaned and allowed to air-dry completely. Keep the foam out of the washer and dryer, since excessive water and high heat can damage its structure. My final thoughts The Layla BioCrystal Side Sleeper Pillow is a strong option for side sleepers who want structured support, a higher profile and the ability to adjust the height. The shoulder cutout gives it an advantage over traditional rectangular pillows, especially if you tend to wake up with neck or shoulder discomfort. Back and stomach sleepers may prefer the Layla BioCrystal Classic Pillow. My husband sleeps on it every night and appreciates its plush support, adjustable loft and roomy design, which keeps his head and neck comfortably supported when he’s lying on his back.

articles.title: Oberlin College professor and wife found fatally shot at home; son charged with murder
articles.summary: A beloved Oberlin College professor and his wife were fatally shot in their Ohio home Wednesday, police said.
articles.body: A beloved Oberlin College professor and his wife were fatally shot in their Ohio home Wednesday, police said. His 31-year-old son has been arrested on murder charges. The body of Pipo Hieu Nguyen-Duy, 64, was found on the first floor of the couple’s home after police conducted a welfare check. His wife, Tran Thi Phong, 56, was found dead in an upstairs bedroom, according to a police incident report. Police said is appears both had been shot. Police identified the suspect as Daniel Jones, of Ashland, Oregon. At an arraignment Thursday, Jones asked the judge to use gender-neutral pronouns and said they go by the name Asia Nguyen-Duy. The investigation began just before 9 a.m. Wednesday, when Oberlin officers responded to the Oberlin College Conservatory parking lot for a report of a smoldering vehicle. The incident report states that the silver Toyota hatchback, which had Oregon license plates, had a boarded-up window and a pipe sticking out of the roof. Nguyen-Duy’s son was identified as the vehicle’s owner, but was not in the area. They were located two blocks away around 10:19 a.m. and taken into custody without incident, police said. Based on officers’ interaction with the son, police conducted a welfare check at the family’s home. Nguyen-Duy and Phong, the son’s stepmother, were located after police forced their way inside, according to the incident report. The son was charged with six counts of murder, four counts of felonious assault and one count of tampering with evidence. An attorney did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday. A motive is unclear. Asia Nguyen-Duy’s arraignment began with officers carrying them into the courtroom in handcuffs and ankle restraints, NBC affiliate WKYC of Cleveland reported. The prosecutor said ammunition was found in Asia Nguyen-Duy’s car. The prosecutor also said that Asia Nguyen-Duy had knocked on the door of an Oberlin resident and asked the woman to record a video to post online. In the video, Asia Nguyen-Duy said they were escaping a cult and said, “everything I did was on my own accord and I take full responsibility,” according to the prosecutor. Police were called to the area for a report of a disheveled person and found Asia Nguyen-Duy with scratches on their face and injuries to their arm and hand, the prosecutor said. Asia Nguyen-Duy told police they had killed their family and gave them the address to the family home, according to the prosecutor. The weapon used in the shooting has not been found. The judge set bond at $3 million bond, citing the egregious nature of the crime. Asia Nguyen-Duy’s biological mother declined to comment, saying she was too upset. Oberlin College remembered the elder Nguyen-Duy as a “beloved professor” of studio art and photography, who had taught at the school since 1998. “During his years at Oberlin, he touched all of us through his passion for photography,” the college’s president Carmen Twillie Ambar said in a statement. She called him “a cherished colleague and a vibrant presence in the classroom and throughout campus.” Nguyen-Duy was born in Hue, Vietnam, and immigrated to the U.S. as a political refugee, according to a biography on his website. He received several awards and grants, including a Guggenheim Fellowship in Photography, and his work has been exhibited in public collections in the U.S., Europe and Asia, the website states.

articles.title: Designed to cripple, not sink: How limpet mines hit tanker with 27 Indians
articles.summary: A Panama-flagged oil tanker carrying 27 Indian seafarers was targeted with limpet mines in the Strait of Hormuz, raising fresh concerns over the safety of
articles.body: A Panama-flagged oil tanker carrying 27 Indian seafarers was targeted with limpet mines in the Strait of Hormuz, raising fresh concerns over the safety of commercial shipping in the strategic waterway. The explosives, reportedly attached to the vessel's hull by a small craft, damaged its engine room and temporarily disabled the tanker before the fire was brought under control.The attack on MT Louise 1 on October 30 was described by maritime security sources as the first known successful use of limpet mines against a vessel in the region since the US-Iran conflict began in February. The incident came a day after another tanker, Liberia-flagged MT Arzanah, carrying two Indian nationals, was targeted in a separate projectile attack.Union minister for ports, shipping and waterways Sarbananda Sonowal said all 29 Indian seafarers aboard the two vessels were safe, with no injuries reported. “All 29 Indian seafarers across both vessels are completely safe with no injuries. We are continuously monitoring the situations & coordinating with the ship management companies to ensure the ongoing security and wellbeing of our crew,” he said.What are limpet mines and how do they work?Limpet mines are small explosive devices designed to attach themselves to the hull of a ship, usually with the help of magnets. They are named after limpets, a type of shellfish that clings tightly to rocks and is difficult to remove.According to The New York Times, the explosives are generally placed manually by swimmers, divers or frogmen. Unlike conventional naval mines, which may be anchored underwater or float near the surface, limpet mines are specifically designed to stick to their targets.They typically contain relatively small explosive charges and use a fuze, a mechanism that triggers detonation, often through a time-delay system. Some versions also have anti-removal mechanisms that can trigger an explosion if someone attempts to detach them.Their primary purpose is not necessarily to sink a vessel but to cause what naval experts call a 'mission kill', damaging critical components and rendering a ship unable to operate.According to Naval Technology, the MILA is a smart limpet mine featuring a computer-controlled detonation system. It can be attached to a ship's hull by divers and can also be used as a demolition charge. Its conical shape and low underwater weight reduce hydrodynamic resistance, making it easier for divers to carry and deploy.Why are they difficult to detect?Limpet mines pose a particular threat because small boats can approach commercial vessels without immediately attracting suspicion. Tankers routinely operate alongside smaller craft in busy shipping lanes, potentially allowing attackers to get close enough to attach explosives.The New York Times noted that placing such devices on moving vessels is considerably more difficult than targeting ships at anchor or moored at ports.Their underwater placement also makes them particularly destructive. Water surrounding the explosive helps direct the force of the blast towards the ship's hull, potentially creating significant damage even with a relatively small charge.The latest incident has highlighted the vulnerability of commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important oil-export routes. Greece-based maritime risk management group Marisks described the tactic as “cheap, low tech and very efficient”.While maritime security sources have attributed the attack to limpet mines, responsibility for the incident remains unclear.

articles.title: Ministers vow online safety action after 18-year-old sextortion victim took own life
articles.summary: Cai Davies died after he had sent messages to a woman he believed had a romantic interest in him.
articles.body:
The UK government has said it remains committed to making the online world as safe as possible for young people following the death of a teenager who took his own life after he fell victim to an online sextortion scam.

Cai Davies, 18, died in June 2025 after he had sent messages to a woman he believed had a romantic interest in him.

South Wales Central Coroner's Court heard he had been targeted by scammers operating from Africa, who demanded money from him and said intimate photos would be sent to his friends and posted on YouTube.

The coroner addressed a Regulation 28 preventing future deaths report to the UK and Welsh government with her concerns about how Cai had fallen victim to the scam.

Assistant coroner Rachel Knight recorded a conclusion of suicide after Davies, from Pontypridd, Rhondda Cynon Taf, died.

Knight said it was "more likely than not" that personal stresses in his life together with falling victim to the sextortion scam "more than minimally contributed" to his death.

She wrote of the scammers: "Conversation quickly turned sexual and she asked him for intimate images, which were then used to blackmail him for money by threatening to send the images to his family and friends, and to upload them to a YouTube channel.

"The images were indeed sent to at least one of Cai's Facebook friends by the scammer.

"Cai was bombarded with video calls and messages via Facebook Messenger and WhatsApp over a very short period of time making demands for money."

Online Safety Minister Ian Murray set out several recent measures the UK government had taken to protect children and young people.

These included criminalising the taking of intimate images without consent, a requirement for online platforms to remove those images, and the introduction of the Online Safety Act.

Murray wrote: "The circumstances surrounding Cai's death are profoundly troubling and I am grateful to you for drawing these matters to my attention.

"As the minister responsible, the government and I are fully committed to making the online world as safe as it can be for everyone, especially children and young people."

The Welsh government said issues around telecommunications and internet services were reserved to Westminster but Senedd ministers were committed to reducing online harm in Wales.

Education Minister Anna Brychan and Culture Minister Heledd Fychan said: "The Welsh government will continue to engage with the UK government and Ofcom on current and emerging online safety risks and their implications for devolved responsibilities.

"We are considering the implications for devolved responsibilities of legislative proposals by the UK government relating to children and young people's access to social media and certain high-risk online features."

They added the Welsh government would "continue to consider emerging evidence, including about the potential effects of online safety measures on suicide prevention and self harm and the risks of unintended consequences".

Brychan and Fychan said the Welsh government would be reviewing existing guidance as well as developing fresh online safety guidance for schools and a new national online safety programme.

"These actions will form part of the Welsh government's wider commitment to strengthening digital resilience, preventing harm and helping people affected by online exploitation to access appropriate support.

"We will continue to review our approach as the evidence and nature of online risks develop," they added.

articles.title: 'Surreal' for Dorset's Lloren to hear song on Celebrity Traitors
articles.summary: Lloren has had three of her songs featured during some of series two's most explosive moments.
articles.body:
"I love murder mystery and binge watched with my partner and I'm absolutely hooked, I love it!"

The new series of Celebrity Traitors has had its fair share of dramatic moments and shock reveals, but its soundtrack has done much to create the moody atmosphere, with its brooding covers and cinematic compositions.

Dorset singer-songwriter Lloren, real name Lauren Bannon, has had three of her songs featured during some of series two's most explosive moments.

"It was only this series that I was like 'do you know what, I need to watch this' because... I thought this, this sounds like a bit of me," she said in the countdown to the show's explosive finale .

Lloren studied music production at Southampton Solent University, with her influences including Lana del Rey, Taylor Swift, and Sigrid.

She first came to the nation's attention in 2018 when she reached The Voice UK final , and released her debut album It's Always Sunny in LA last year.

The songwriter has had her music featured in shows ranging from Grey's Anatomy and I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here to Love Island.

Lloren's songs on Celebrity Traitors were made with Power-Haus Creative, a company that works with composers and recording artists, often on music for programmes and trailer music.

Remember My Name, also produced and composed by Berlin Aires and Jonathon Deering, featured during the pivotal moment when mathematician and celebrity faithful Hannah Fry was given an ultimatum to join the traitors.

"Sometimes [songs] just come because you're just feeling a certain way," Lloren told BBC Dorset Breakfast show presenter Steve Harris.

"Then other times, like at a songwriting camp that I did, we were given briefs and told 'make things that may be dark or a bit sinister' and so I just channelled my inner diva and thought, you know, 'they'll remember my name'.

"So that specific song was written with the idea in mind. It needed to be moody and that it would probably land on something.

"I didn't know what it would land on, didn't know it would be Traitors, but I knew it's got to be a dark scene, I've got to channel this sort of energy."

The song's use on the programme, which this year had its biggest launch yet , still came as a pleasant surprise.

"They don't warn me beforehand - with a lot of ITV and BBC stuff it's called blanket cover, and quite often you get no indication that you're going to be on it, and I must have a fan in the music supervisor realm."

She added: "I hadn't really watched The Traitors until this series which is crazy to me because I love murder mystery. I'm a big murder mystery fan.

"I just hadn't got round to do it... and I've been hooked.

"Also my friend Sean Stealth, he had one as well and I recognised the track instantly and I was like 'oh I think this is my friend' and then me and my partner were watching, and I was like 'do you know what? I did backing vocals for this'.

"Actually me and a group of us that were at a songwriting camp in France had done the backing vocals for it so that was quite a surreal moment.

"Anytime I see my song on TV it's surreal and I have to pinch myself."

articles.title: Great white shark makes terrifyingly close pass by fisherman in kayak in shocking video
articles.summary: Helmet camera video from David Slavich's fishing kayak captures a massive great white shark gliding dangerously past him in Bay Area waters.
articles.body: There are few activities in this world more relaxing than fishing. I think we all can agree there is something very zen—like in grabbing a line, a pole, and some bait and just being one with nature for a morning. One man thought he was going to have a nice, peaceful afternoon on the ocean in his kayak until his day of solo fishing was rudely interrupted by someone with some serious personal space issues. SHARK BITES FISHERMAN TWICE DURING KAYAKING ENCOUNTER ALONG CALIFORNIA BEACH And this wasn't a fellow fisherman or some drunk guy in his Boston Whaler. Hell, it wasn't even a human being. That's right, a massive great white shark buzzed some poor kayaker just trying to enjoy his day off, and the whole thing was caught on the fisherman's helmet camera. Footage from the fisherman, David Slavich, shows him getting startled as the giant predator closed in. "The shark came incredibly close, swimming alongside me just beneath the surface," Slavich told Storyful, adding that he was "absolutely amazed" by its size. "There was a moment when it seemed like we were looking directly at each other, and I had the distinct feeling that it was just as curious about me as I was about it," Slavich said. 10-FOOT GREAT WHITE SHARK SPOTTED SWIMMING DANGEROUSLY CLOSE TO YOUNG PEOPLE "I felt more awe and fascination than fear," he said. "It’s an experience I’ll never forget." You don't even see the shark coming at first, but you can hear the terrified words trembling out of Slavich's mouth. "Oh my God! Oh my God," he repeats as the great white makes its way into the frame of the video. In a split-second decision that might have saved his life - or at the very least, a limb or two - Slavich reels his line in quickly to ensure the shark doesn't take the bait and pull him in with it. As the monster with teeth glides past, we get a full view of its size, appearing to be about as big as Slavich's kayak. Once the shark passes by harmlessly, Slavich utters a phrase I think we can all relate to in a situation like that. "Okay, we're getting the f--- out of here," he exclaims. articles.title: In 2022, Arlington County, Virginia, turned a reclaimed 50-foot turbine blade into The Pike, a gateway sculpture paired with 4,784 coins representing 117 countries
articles.summary: Discover Arlington County's unique sculpture, \"The Pike,\" a 50-foot art piece made from a reclaimed wind turbine blade, symbolizing cultural diversity with 4,784 coins from 117 countries. Explore its historical significance and artistic inspiration.
articles.body: Receiving travellers with a cordial welcome at the western gateway near Bailey’s Crossroads sits "The Pike." Public Art Services installed the public artwork in 2022 at Columbia Pike and South Jefferson Street. According to Arlington’s official record, the artwork was conceived by Donald Lipski from a salvaged turbine wing, completed with concrete and steel. The structure’s hallmark lies in its base, which is made of coins representing 117 countries, contributed by every continent with the exception of Antarctica.A sculpture based on the history of Columbia PikeThe Pike is a work that uses a salvaged turbine wing as its main component, which measures 50 feet in height. Because of its unique shape, Lipski specifically chose a wind turbine wing, which also nods to the creation of North America’s first windmill in Virginia in the 1600s. The supporting base of the structure is reinforced by concrete and steel, while its surface is embellished with hundreds of coins.The sculpture derives inspiration from the historical meaning and significance of the word pike itself. It plays on the concept of the pike as a weapon, which was originally held horizontally as a signal to travellers to stop. Instead, Lipski’s interpretation of the word places the turbine wing vertically, as a way of suggesting an open toll gate. Historically, the road is one of the oldest thoroughfares in the region; as per Arlington County, its construction was authorised in 1810 by the United States Congress to connect outlying areas with the District of Columbia.The sculpture was commissioned by the county in tandem with its Multimodal Street Improvement project. The position it holds at Columbia Pike and South Jefferson Street cements its standing as a marker for the western entrance to Arlington from Fairfax County. Essentially, it established a connection between a reclaimed turbine wing and a road whose history predates the artwork.All the coins were collected from residentsThe base of the sculpture holds a total of 4,784 coins, which were donated by Arlington County residents, and together these coins originated from 117 countries and every continent with the exception of Antarctica. Before the coins became part of the installation, they were collected, counted, and sorted by the residents.The coins form an arrangement that alludes to the time when Columbia Pike was used as a toll road. The international origins of the coins are reflective of the county's description of Arlington as an ethnically diverse community. In essence, the sculpture bridges the past and present by using toll-inspired coins to honour the county’s transport history while celebrating the international origins of people living along Columbia Pike.All of this aligned with the artist’s intention for the site, which was to turn it into a welcoming landmark. In an account by Public Art Services, Lipski described his interest in making an artwork that would be imbued into the everyday lives of the residents. For people returning to Arlington, the sculpture would indicate that they had finally arrived home.Lipski’s installation isn’t the only piece of history to grace the county; just less than 0.1 miles south of the Pike, a sandstone boundary stone stands in the median of South Jefferson Street. The marker is part of a series installed in 1791 and 1792 to mark the perimeter of the original District of Columbia, which covered ten miles square.
